awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Sugar Based Microparticles for Robust Treatment of Diseases
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the exploration of sugar based microparticles for accelerating metabolism in immunotherapies. This proposed technology is a drug delivery vehicle that can transport the drug of interest to immune cells, for which the healthcare and oncology industry can make use of. The drug delivery vehicle is constituted from a metabolite, allowing for increased energy levels of cells. This would be important for showing how metabolic pathways can induce a cure. Access to such a drug delivery technology has the potential to cure many patients. The technology can generate products that can improve cancer immunotherapies in patients with solid tumors. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of microparticles that can accelerate metabolism of specific immune cells to develop cancer immunotherapies. This technology will help in developing advanced cellular therapies so that they can effectively fight cancer. The microparticles are made of small molecules that can insert themselves in specific metabolic pathway of immune cells and thus elevate their need to be dependent on outside sources of nutrition in the tumor microenvironment. This technology can transform the cellular therapy space and develop a highly translational product for cancer immunotherapy.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Cellular therapy represents one of the most exciting frontiers in modern medicine. CAR T cell therapy has already cured patients with certain blood cancers who had no other options. It is now being explored for autoimmune diseases, solid tumors, and other conditions. However, its high cost, manufacturing complexity, and the challenge of T cell exhaustion limit its reach. Research like that conducted at CWRU aims to make cellular therapy more effective, more accessible, and more affordable.

The NSF I-Corps program is built on a simple but powerful idea. Great science alone is not enough. To truly help patients, a technology must find its right customer, solve a real problem, and navigate a clear path to market. The program challenged the team to step outside the laboratory and listen. They conducted over 100 interviews with oncologists, hematologists, cell therapy manufacturers, regulatory experts, investors, and entrepreneurs. 

The single greatest lesson was the importance of listening before building. Early assumptions about who needed the technology and why were repeatedly challenged and refined. The team learned that smaller CAR T cell companies are more accessible and more open to innovation than large pharmaceutical giants. They learned that the path from laboratory discovery to patient treatment is long, expensive, and filled with regulatory complexity. They learned that a technology's value is ultimately defined not by its elegance in the laboratory but by the problem it solves for a real customer.

At the heart of this project lies a fascinating and rapidly growing field called immunometabolism. This discipline studies how the energy state of immune cells determines their ability to fight disease. Just as a soldier cannot fight on an empty stomach, a CAR T cell cannot destroy cancer if it runs out of fuel. The team's research focuses on providing immune cells with the metabolic support they need to remain powerful, persistent, and effective. This approach is novel, practical, and broadly applicable across many diseases beyond cancer.

The NSF I-Corps program gave this research a direction, a voice, and a purpose beyond the laboratory. And the patients who may one day benefit from this work are the reason it matters.
